questions.title: How does the 'likelihood of success on the merits' factor differ between the § 1182(f) challenge and the APA challenge in this stay order?
questions.question_body: I am confused by how the Ninth Circuit applied the *Nken* stay factors differently to the two distinct claims in this case. For the challenge to Executive Order 14163 under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f), the court says the government is 'likely to prevail' citing *Trump v. Hawaii* and the deference owed to the President's finding of detriment. However, for the APA challenge regarding the defunding of resettlement services, the court says the government is 'not likely to prevail.' Can someone explain how a single panel can reach opposite conclusions on 'likelihood of success' within the same order? Does this mean the statutory interpretation of § 1522 overrides the broad discretion usually given to the executive in immigration matters?

questions.title: Is 8 U.S.C. § 1522 a mandatory spending statute or a discretionary authorization, and how does the 'available appropriations' clause affect this?
questions.question_body: The majority opinion seems to treat 8 U.S.C. § 1522 as imposing a mandatory duty on the Director of ORR to provide reception and placement services, ordering the reinstatement of cooperative agreements. However, Judge Lee's dissent argues that the statute is merely an 'authorization,' pointing to the title of the section and the repeated use of 'authorized' in subsections (b) through (e). The majority relies on subsection (a)'s use of 'shall,' but qualifies it with 'to the extent of available appropriations.' Since Congress did appropriate funds (even if reduced by a rescission), does the presence of appropriated money automatically turn an 'authorized' program into a 'mandatory' one? How do courts typically distinguish between statutes that say an agency 'may' do something versus those that say it 'shall' do something 'to the extent of available appropriations'?

questions.title: What is the procedural effect of vacating previous stays while simultaneously issuing a new 'stay pending appeal' with a specific carveout?
questions.question_body: The operative paragraph of this order is procedurally dense. The court vacates its prior administrative stay (July 18) and its prior partial stay (March 25, as amended). It then states that the District Court's preliminary injunctions are 'stayed in their entirety, except as noted below.' The exception is a directive for the government to reinstate cooperative agreements for refugees already admitted. Procedurally, does this mean the District Court's injunction blocking the refugee ban remains inactive (because it is stayed), while only the injunction regarding domestic services is active? How does this hybrid approach work practically? Is this effectively a modification of the stay rather than a simple grant or denial?

questions.title: Does *Trump v. Hawaii*'s deference to presidential findings under § 1182(f) prevent judicial review of whether a suspension violates other statutes like the Refugee Act of 1980?
questions.question_body: The majority cites *Trump v. Hawaii* to support staying the injunction against Executive Order 14163, noting that courts cannot engage in a 'searching inquiry' into the President's justification if he finds entry detrimental to US interests. However, Plaintiffs also alleged violations of the Refugee Act of 1980. If § 1182(f) gives such broad power to suspend entry, can that power be limited by later or more specific statutes like the Refugee Act? Why did the court seem to bypass any potential conflict between § 1182(f) and the Refugee Act when analyzing likelihood of success for EO 14163, whereas they dug deep into statutory text for § 1522?

questions.title: Can a court order an agency to reinstate specific contractors/cooperative agreements as a remedy for failing to provide statutorily required services?
questions.question_body: The court orders: '[T]he government is hereby directed to reinstate such cooperative agreements necessary...' because they are unsure if new agencies can be found in time. I thought courts generally enjoin illegal actions or compel specific performance of duties, but they avoid micromanaging *how* an agency fulfills those duties (e.g., telling them which vendors to hire). By forcing State/HHS to reinstate *prior* agreements rather than just saying 'you must fund services,' is this order crossing into administrative management territory? Is this level of specificity common in preliminary relief stages involving complex procurement processes?

questions.title: How does Judge Lee reconcile his agreement on Presidential authority under § 1182(f) with his dissent regarding domestic service mandates under § 1522?
questions.question_body: Judge Lee concurs that President Trump has vast discretion under § 1082(f) regarding border closure/suspension but dissents on whether domestic services are mandatory under § 1522. He argues that even if funds exist ('appropriations flow'), Congress used permissive language ('authorized') meaning no cause exists until affirmative steps are taken by Congress or Agency heads beyond mere appropriation availability? Is there precedent where appropriations alone create rights without explicit mandatory language elsewhere in statute.
